day_title: The Cost You Stopped Adding Up
reflection_question: Write down what this has actually cost you so far - money, time, trust, opportunities, people. Do not round down.
devotional_text:
There is a number you have stopped working out.

You used to know roughly what it cost. At some point you stopped checking, because checking made it real.

Today we are going to check.

Not to beat you up. There is no point in that, and it does not work anyway — shame has never once gotten anybody sober.

We are checking because **you cannot want out of a place you keep describing as not that bad.**

# A Son Who Did The Maths Too Late

Jesus tells a story about a young man who asks his father for his inheritance early.

Think about what that actually means. It means: *I wish you were dead, and I want the money now.*

And the father gives it to him.

> "Not many days after, the younger son gathered all of this together and traveled into a far country. There he wasted his property with riotous living." (Luke 15:13)

Far country. That is a good description of where this takes you.

Not a decision to leave. A drift. A series of small moves, each one reasonable at the time, until one day you look up and you are a long way from anybody who knows you.

## Then The Money Runs Out

> "When he had spent all of it, there arose a severe famine in that country, and he began to be in need." (Luke 15:14)

Notice the order.

He spent it all first. *Then* the famine came.

If the famine had come while he still had money, he would have been fine. He had no margin left, so an ordinary bad season turned into a catastrophe.

That is what this does to a life. It eats your margin. Your savings, your sleep, your patience, the goodwill people had for you. So that when something normal goes wrong — a bill, an illness, an argument — there is nothing left to absorb it.

## How Far It Went

> "He went and joined himself to one of the citizens of that country, and he sent him into his fields to feed pigs. He wanted to fill his belly with the husks that the pigs ate, but no one gave him any." (Luke 15:15-16)

For a Jewish listener this is as low as the story could possibly go. Pigs were unclean. He is not just poor, he is in a place he would once have found unthinkable.

And here is the line that should stop you:

**He wanted to eat the pigs' food.**

He did not arrive at that wanting it. He arrived there one reasonable step at a time.

Ask yourself what you do now that you would have found unthinkable three years ago. Everybody in this fight has an answer. The answer is the measure of the drift.

## And Then Four Words

> "But when he came to himself..." (Luke 15:17)

Came to himself.

As though he had been somewhere else. As though the person making those decisions was not quite him.

Anyone who has lived inside this knows that feeling precisely. There is the you that decides, and the you that wakes up and has to live with it.

The turn starts the moment those two meet.

## What He Actually Thinks About

He does not have a spiritual experience. He gets practical.

> "How many hired servants of my father's have bread enough to spare, and I'm dying with hunger!" (Luke 15:17)

He compares. He remembers that somewhere, things are not like this.

That is what an honest count does. Not despair. Comparison. *It is not supposed to be like this, and I know that because I have seen better.*

## The Father Was Already Looking

> "But while he was still far off, his father saw him, and was moved with compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him." (Luke 15:20)

The son had a speech ready. He had rehearsed it on the road.

He got about one sentence out before the father interrupted with a robe, a ring and a party.

**The father saw him while he was still far off** — which means the father had been watching the road. For a long time. Every day.

You are going to count the cost today. Do it knowing how this story ends, because it does not end with a lecture.

## What To Watch For In Luke 15:11-24

* 💸 What the son asks for in verse 12, and what the father does
* 🧭 The words "far country" in verse 13
* 📉 The order of events in verse 14 — spent everything, then famine
* 🐖 How low verse 16 goes, and that he got there gradually
* 👁️ Who sees whom first in verse 20
* 🎉 How much of the son's rehearsed speech the father lets him finish

## The Bigger Takeaway

You have been protecting yourself from the number.

But the number is not your enemy. The number is the thing that makes you want out.

The son did not change because somebody shamed him. He changed because he finally looked honestly at where he was and remembered that it was not supposed to be like this.

**And the second he turned around, he found out his father had been watching the road the whole time.**

## Today's One Thing

**Write the real count.**

Four columns. Be specific. No rounding down.

* 💷 **Money.** A rough figure. Per week, then multiply it by how long this has been going on. Write the total even if it makes you feel sick.
* ⏳ **Hours.** Doing it, recovering from it, hiding it, thinking about it.
* 🤝 **Trust.** Name the people who used to believe what you said and now check.
* 🚪 **Missed.** The job, the trip, the morning, the conversation, the relationship.

This is one of the harder tasks in the sixty days. Do it once, properly, and keep it.

And when you are done, read Luke 15:20 again before you close the page. Do not leave yourself sitting in the count.

## Today's Prayer

Father,

I have known for a long time what this is costing and I have refused to add it up.

I did not want to see it written down, because then I would have to do something about it.

So I looked at the number today, and it is worse than I let myself believe.

I do not know how to fix most of what is on that list. Some of it I cannot get back.

But the son in Your story could not fix any of it either. He just got up and went home.

I am a long way off. Keep watching the road.

In Jesus' name, amen.

day_title: What It Looks Like From The Outside
reflection_question: Who in your life has already noticed? What do you think they see that you have been explaining away?
devotional_text:
There is a passage in Proverbs that is nearly three thousand years old and reads like it was written last week.

It is about a man and his drink. But anyone fighting anything will recognise themselves in it, and the last line is the most accurate sentence about addiction in the Bible.

Let us walk through it slowly.

# It Opens With Questions

> "Who has woe? Who has sorrow? Who has strife? Who has complaints? Who has needless bruises? Who has bloodshot eyes?" (Proverbs 23:29)

Six questions, and not one of them is about drinking.

They are about the *wreckage*. Sorrow. Arguments. Unexplained injuries. The look of somebody's face.

This is how it shows up to everybody else. Not as the thing itself — you have hidden that fairly well — but as a pattern of damage they cannot account for.

**Needless bruises.** Marks you cannot explain, or explain too quickly.

Then the answer:

> "Those who stay long at the wine; those who go to seek out mixed wine." (Proverbs 23:30)

Stay long. Seek out.

It is not the people who have a drink. It is the people who stay, and who go looking.

## Then A Warning About The Beginning

> "Don't look at the wine when it is red, when it sparkles in the cup, when it goes down smoothly. In the end, it bites like a snake, and poisons like a viper." (Proverbs 23:31-32)

Notice the honesty in verse 31.

It sparkles. It goes down smoothly. The Bible is not pretending it is unpleasant.

That is important, because a lot of religious talk about this subject is dishonest in exactly that place. It describes the thing as obviously disgusting, and you know it is not, and so you stop listening to the whole argument.

Scripture does not do that. It says: yes, it is lovely going in, **and look what is at the other end of it.**

The warning is not about the first ten minutes. It is about the end.

## Then The Loss Of Control

> "Your eyes will see strange things, and your mind will imagine confusing things. Yes, you will be as he who lies down in the middle of the sea, or as he who lies on top of the rigging." (Proverbs 23:33-34)

Lying down in the middle of the sea.

Asleep at the top of a ship's mast.

Both pictures are the same idea: **in enormous danger and completely unaware of it.**

That is the part the people who love you can see and you cannot. From where they stand, you are asleep on the rigging. From where you are, everything feels survivable.

## And Then The Last Line

> "They hit me, and I was not hurt! They beat me, and I don't feel it! When will I wake up? I can do it again. I can find another." (Proverbs 23:35)

Read that one more time.

**"When will I wake up? I can do it again."**

That is not a man who has learned anything. That is a man coming round from the last one and already arranging the next.

Three thousand years ago, somebody wrote that down. The pattern is that old and that exact.

## Why This Matters Today

Because you have probably been telling yourself that nobody really knows.

Somebody knows.

Not all of it, maybe. But they have noticed the bruises they cannot explain. The mood on certain evenings. The money that does not add up. The way you get strange about particular questions.

They may never have said it, because people are frightened of saying it wrong.

It is worth sitting with that today, not as humiliation, but as information: **you are less hidden than you think, and the people still standing near you have chosen to stay anyway.**

## What To Watch For In Proverbs 23:29-35

* ❓ That verse 29 asks six questions before it names the cause
* ✨ The honesty of verse 31 — it admits the appeal
* 🐍 What the end is compared to, in verse 32
* ⛵ The two pictures in verse 34, and what they have in common
* 🔁 The last sentence of verse 35, and who is speaking it

## The Bigger Takeaway

From the inside, this feels managed. Private. Mostly under control.

From the outside it looks like somebody asleep on the rigging, and the people watching have been quietly terrified for longer than you know.

You do not have to accept everything anybody says about you. But today, consider the possibility that **their view of this is more accurate than yours**, because they are not the ones making the case for it every evening.

## Today's One Thing

**Name who has already noticed.**

Write down one or two people who you believe have seen something, even if they have never said it directly.

Then write what you think they have seen. Not what you told them. What they actually observed.

You are not confronting anyone. You are not confessing today — that was Day 3's name and it keeps.

You are just stopping the belief that you have gotten away with this, because that belief is load-bearing. It is one of the main things holding the whole structure up.

## Today's Prayer

God,

I have been telling myself that this is my business and that it is not hurting anybody else.

I do not think that is true any more.

There are people who have watched me and worried and said nothing, because they did not know how to start, or because the last time somebody tried I made sure it went badly.

I am sorry for what this has done to them.

Show me what they see. Give me the stomach to look at it without immediately defending myself.

And for the ones who are still here after everything — thank You. I do not know why they stayed.

In Jesus' name, amen.

reflection_question: What do you usually say to yourself the morning after? Write it down, then write what you would say to a friend in the same position.
devotional_text:
You know this feeling better than almost any other.

The first few seconds of being awake before you remember. Then remembering.

Then the familiar voice starting up.

*You did it again. After everything you said. You are pathetic. Nothing is ever going to change.*

Psalm 51 was written on a morning like that.

# Who Wrote It, And After What

David. King of Israel. The man after God's own heart.

He had slept with another man's wife, and when she became pregnant he arranged for her husband to be killed in battle to cover it up.

Then he carried on as normal for the best part of a year, until a prophet walked in and said *you are the man.*

This psalm is what came out of him afterwards.

So when you feel you have gone too far for this to be fixable, understand who is writing the words you are about to read.

## He Does Not Start With Himself

> "Have mercy on me, God, according to your loving kindness. According to the multitude of your tender mercies, blot out my transgressions." (Psalm 51:1)

Look at what he appeals to.

Not *according to how sorry I am*. Not *according to how much I promise to change*.

**According to Your loving kindness. According to Your tender mercies.**

That is the only ground any of us have, and it is better ground than the other kind, because it does not depend on the strength of your remorse — which, let us be honest, has been intense before and changed nothing.

## He Does Not Minimise It Either

> "For I know my transgressions. My sin is constantly before me." (Psalm 51:3)

Constantly before me. He cannot stop seeing it.

You know that too. The replay. The specific details that come back at odd moments.

He does not pretend it was small and he does not pretend it was somebody else's fault. He looks straight at it.

**Honesty and mercy are not opposites. This whole psalm holds both at once, and that is the thing to learn from it.**

## Then He Asks For The Right Thing

This is the verse that matters most for anybody in this fight:

> "Create in me a clean heart, O God. Renew a right spirit within me." (Psalm 51:10)

**Create.** Not repair. Not clean up. Create.

It is the same word used for what God did at the beginning of Genesis, when there was nothing to work with.

David is not asking to be improved. He has tried improvement. He is asking for something to be *made* in him that was not there before.

That is the right prayer for a morning like this. Not "help me do better next time." You have prayed that one. **"Make something in me that is not there yet."**

## And One More Thing He Asks

> "Restore to me the joy of your salvation. Uphold me with a willing spirit." (Psalm 51:12)

Restore the *joy*.

People in this fight lose that early and do not always notice. Faith becomes a thing you are failing at rather than a thing that gives you anything.

He asks for the gladness back. That is allowed. That is in the Bible.

## What God Actually Wants From You Today

> "The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit. A broken and contrite heart, O God, you will not despise." (Psalm 51:17)

**You will not despise.**

Read that in the voice of the thing that has been talking to you since you woke up.

That voice has been telling you that you are disgusting, that God is finished with you, that there is no point praying from here.

Psalm 51:17 says a broken heart is not something God turns away from. It is the one thing He never turns away from.

## What To Watch For In Psalm 51:1-17

* 🙏 What David appeals to in verse 1 — and what he does not
* 👁️ "Constantly before me" in verse 3
* 🆕 The word "create" in verse 10
* 😔 That he asks for *joy* back in verse 12
* 🫀 What God does not despise, in verse 17
* 🗣️ That he talks about telling others, in verse 13, before he has fixed himself

## The Bigger Takeaway

The voice on the morning after is not the voice of God.

God convicts. The other thing condemns. They sound similar and they go in opposite directions: conviction points at the thing and says *come home*, condemnation points at you and says *stay out there, you are what you did*.

David had done something genuinely terrible, and what came back was mercy and a new heart.

**The morning after is not the end of your relationship with God. For David it was the beginning of the most honest part of it.**

## Today's One Thing

**Write the two sentences.**

First: exactly what you say to yourself the morning after. Word for word, including the worst of it.

Second: what you would say to a friend you loved who told you they had done the same thing.

Read them next to each other.

The gap between those two is not humility. It is cruelty that you have gotten used to.

The second sentence is closer to how God speaks. You are allowed to speak to yourself the way you would speak to somebody you love.

## Today's Prayer

God,

I have done it again and I do not have a speech.

I have promised and broken the promise so many times that my own words have stopped meaning anything to me, so I am not going to make another one today.

I am just going to ask for what David asked for.

Not a better version of me. Something new. Make something in me that I cannot make.

And quiet the voice that has been going since I woke up, because it does not sound like You. You said You would not despise a broken heart, and mine is in pieces this morning.

I am still here. Do not let go.

In Jesus' name, amen.

day_title: You Are Not The Only One
reflection_question: What would it mean to believe that there is a way out of the moment, every time, even when you cannot see it?
devotional_text:
One of the cruellest parts of this is how alone it makes you feel.

Not physically alone. You might be surrounded by people.

Alone in the sense that nobody in the room would understand if you said it out loud. Everybody else seems to be managing. You are the only one carrying something this shameful.

That belief is doing a lot of damage, and it is not true.

# A Sentence Written For You

> "No temptation has taken you except what is common to man." (1 Corinthians 10:13)

**Common to man.**

Not rare. Not uniquely disgraceful. Not a special category of broken that only applies to you.

Common.

That word is doing something important. Paul is cutting the legs out from under the isolation, because isolation is where this thing is strongest.

Think about it practically. If your struggle is unique, then nobody can help, nobody has ever come back from it, and there is no point telling anyone. All three of those conclusions keep you exactly where you are.

If it is common, then other people have walked out of it, and some of them are near you right now.

## Who He Was Writing To

It is worth knowing that Paul was not writing to impressive people.

The church at Corinth was a mess. A few chapters earlier he lists what some of them had been — and it is not a gentle list. Then he writes one of the most hopeful sentences in the New Testament about them: *and such were some of you.*

Were.

Past tense.

He is writing to people who got out.

## The Warning Just Before It

> "Therefore let him who thinks he stands be careful that he doesn't fall." (1 Corinthians 10:12)

Do not skip this one, because it is the other half.

The people most likely to fall are the ones who have decided they are past it.

You will have good weeks in the next fifty days. Somewhere around a strong week, a thought will arrive: *I have actually beaten this now. I could probably handle a little.*

That thought has ended more recoveries than any craving ever has.

**Standing is not the same as being finished.**

## And Then The Promise

> "God is faithful, who will not allow you to be tempted above what you are able, but will with the temptation also make the way of escape, that you may be able to endure it." (1 Corinthians 10:13)

Two things in there, and people usually only hear the first.

The first is that it will not exceed what you can bear. Honestly, on a bad night that sentence can feel like an insult, because it has absolutely felt like more than you could bear.

So look at the second part, which is more practical.

**With the temptation, a way of escape.**

Not instead of it. *With* it. At the same time, in the same moment, there is a door.

It is usually unglamorous. It is a phone in your hand. It is walking out of the room. It is the name you wrote down on Day 3. It is going to bed. It is the drive you do not take.

The door is rarely impressive and it is almost never comfortable. But the promise is that it is there, every time, and part of the work of the next fifty days is learning to look for it instead of standing still and arguing with yourself.

## What To Watch For In 1 Corinthians 10:1-13

* 🏜️ That Paul uses Israel in the wilderness as the example — a whole nation that struggled
* ⚠️ The warning in verse 12, aimed at people who feel secure
* 👥 "Common to man" in verse 13
* 🚪 The way of escape, and the word "with"
* 💪 What the escape is *for* — "that you may be able to endure it"

## The Bigger Takeaway

You are not a special case.

That sounds like an insult and it is one of the kindest things in this study.

Being a special case means no help, no precedent, no hope. Being common means there is a road, other people have walked it, and there are doors in the walls of the rooms you keep getting stuck in.

**Every single time, there is a way out of the moment. Your job is not to be strong enough. Your job is to look for the door.**

## Today's One Thing

**Decide your door in advance.**

You cannot invent an escape plan at the moment of craving. Your judgement is worst exactly then.

So pick it now, while you are calm, and make it specific:

* 📵 "I put my phone in the kitchen and go to bed."
* 🚶 "I put my shoes on and walk to the end of the road and back."
* 📞 "I text ______ the single word we agreed, even at 2 a.m."
* 🚿 "I get in the shower."
* 🔑 "I give my car keys to my wife at 8 p.m."

One door. Written down. Somewhere you will see it.

It will feel too small to work. Do it anyway. The purpose is not to be a solution; the purpose is to put ninety seconds between the thought and the act, and ninety seconds is often the whole fight.

## Today's Prayer

God,

I have believed for a long time that I am the worst version of this, and that if anybody really knew, they would be done with me.

Your word says this is common to man. That other people have stood exactly here.

I do not feel that. Help me believe it anyway.

And when the moment comes — and it is coming, probably sooner than I want to think about — show me the door. Make me look for it instead of standing there negotiating.

I am not asking to stop feeling it. I am asking to see the way out while I am feeling it.

You said You are faithful. I am going to need that to be true tonight.

In Jesus' name, amen.

reflection_question: Is there anything left that you have not told God about this? Say it now, in your own words, and write down how it felt to.
devotional_text:
This is the last day of the first part.

Nine days ago you said the real name of it. Since then you have looked at the lie you tell yourself, the weight of the secret, what you are actually thirsty for, why trying harder keeps failing, what it has cost, what it looks like from outside, the morning after, and the fact that you are not alone in it.

That is a lot of honesty for ten days. Most people never do it at all.

Today we close the part by handing all of it over.

# The Psalm That Knows Too Much

Psalm 139 can be uncomfortable if you are hiding something.

> "Yahweh, you have searched me, and you know me. You know my sitting down and my rising up. You perceive my thoughts from afar." (Psalm 139:1-2)

He knows when you sit down and when you get up.

Which means He knows about the evenings. He knows what time you usually start. He knows the route you take and the shop you stop at and the tab you open.

> "For there is not a word on my tongue, but, behold, Yahweh, you know it altogether." (Psalm 139:4)

Every promise you made Him and broke. He heard all of them.

## Now Here Is The Part That Changes It

If that was the whole psalm it would be unbearable. It is not.

David goes on to ask where he could possibly go to get away from God — heaven, the grave, the far side of the sea — and finds there is nowhere.

And then he says this about the darkest place he can think of:

> "Even the darkness doesn't hide from you, but the night shines as the day. The darkness is like light to you." (Psalm 139:12)

Here is what matters.

**David does not write that as a threat. He writes it as comfort.**

The whole psalm is a man finding out he cannot get away from God and being *relieved*.

Because the alternative — a God who could not find you in the dark, who lost track of you somewhere in the last few years, who is only available in the clean parts of your life — that God would be no use to you at all.

You do not need a God who is impressed by you. You need one who can follow you into the worst hour of your week.

## Why This Is The Right Place To End Part One

There is one more thing people hold back.

After all the honesty, there is usually still a corner. The bit that is too humiliating, or too recent, or involves somebody else, or feels like it would make God turn away if He really heard it.

And you have been praying around it. Close to it. Never quite into it.

Psalm 139 removes the point of that. He already knows. The only thing your silence is achieving is distance.

## How David Finishes

After all of that, knowing he is completely seen, he asks for *more* of it:

> "Search me, God, and know my heart. Try me, and know my thoughts. See if there is any wicked way in me, and lead me in the everlasting way." (Psalm 139:23-24)

That is an extraordinary prayer from somebody who has just established that God sees everything.

He is saying: show me what I cannot see in myself. Including the parts I am still defending.

That is not the prayer of a man who feels safe because he is good. It is the prayer of a man who feels safe because of who he is talking to.

## What To Watch For In Psalm 139:1-24

* 👣 How ordinary the things are that God knows in verses 2 and 3 — sitting, rising, lying down
* 🌍 Every place David tries to imagine being out of reach, in verses 7 to 10
* 🌑 What verse 12 says about darkness, and the tone he says it in
* 🧵 That he goes back to being made in verses 13 to 16, before he was anything
* 🙋 That after all that, he asks to be searched *more*

## The Bigger Takeaway

You have spent years managing what people can see.

There is one relationship where that was never possible, and you have been behaving as though it was.

**Nothing you say today will be news to Him.** The only thing that changes when you say it is that you stop being alone with it.

That is what the first ten days have been for. Not to fix anything. To stop the hiding, so that there is something real for God to work with.

Tomorrow we start looking at who He actually is when He finds you.

## Today's One Thing

**Tell Him the last part.**

The bit you have held back. Out loud if you possibly can — there is something about hearing your own voice say it that writing does not do.

Not a summary. The specific thing. The detail that makes you wince.

You do not need religious language. You do not need to explain or justify it. You are not informing Him; you are stopping the pretending in the one relationship where pretending has never once worked.

Then finish the way David did. Ask Him to show you whatever else is in there that you cannot see yourself.

And then sit for a minute without asking for anything.

## Today's Prayer

God,

You already know. All of it. The parts I said out loud this week and the part I did not.

I have been praying around the edge of it for years, and I think I believed that if I never said it directly, it was somehow less real.

So here it is, in plain words, with nothing taken out.

I am not going to promise You anything today, because my promises have not been worth much.

I am just not hiding any more.

Search me. Show me what else is in me that I cannot see. I would rather know than keep defending it.

And thank You that the darkness is not dark to You, because that is where I have been living, and I needed You to be able to see in here.

In Jesus' name, amen.
